title: addressing mental health resource deficiencies in pacific rim countries
display_name: Addressing mental health resource deficiencies in Pacific Rim countries
abstract: the past 100 years have seen an enormous expansion of knowledge about mental disorders and interventions that can prevent them, cure them, or alleviate their course and improve their outcome. neuroscience advances brought us information about the functioning of the central nervous system and processes that lead to mental illness. behavioral sciences made major contributions to our understanding of factors that can contribute to the occurrence of mental disorders or influence their treatment. clinical experience has contributed to improved care in many countries, and the sharing of knowledge about matters relevant to psychiatric illnesses and their treatments has reached an unprecedented level. yet, despite these vast advances of knowledge, mentally ill individuals in developed countries and most of the population of the poor and developing countries do not receive adequate care. these individuals and their families, therefore, suffer from their disorders far more than necessary. in a vast majority of cases, those with psychiatric illnesses do not receive the benefits of care, which is based on the most up-to-date knowledge about psychiatric illness and its treatment. among the reasons for this situation, several stand out prominently. the stigmatization of the mentally ill reduces the value that people with mental illness have in the eyes of individuals, communities, and societal decision-makers, and mental health programs, therefore, have low priority and are given far too little when resource allocation decisions are made. the resulting poor state of psychiatric care then acts as a deterrent and makes young graduates reluctant to select psychiatry or other mental health professions as their career. further, the increasing complexity of labor and competitiveness of societies reduces the chances of the mentally ill or intellectually disabled to find a job and create an independent life. in many instances, borders of language, culture, tradition, and political systems prevent the universal application of highly effective methods of detection and treatment of mental illnesses. many other reasons for the insufficiency of mental health care and poor state of psychiatry in several countries could be listed and have been well described in numerous publications. the problems, however, do not arise from environmental forces only. psychiatry and our allied professional partners are also at fault for often being slow to respond to the array of well recognized forces that influence psychiatric care in the development of innovative strategies for mental health care adjusted to the current socioeconomic-political situation. the strategies of community health care, for example, have not changed substantially in recent decades in ways adequate to keep pace with well recognized emerging needs, although the nature of communities and their functioning has undergone substantial changes. the hopes that primary health care, as presently structured, would be helpful in providing a needed adjunct to deliver psychiatric services, has not been found to be true and has been abandoned or extensively modified in most environments. community care approaches are not only difficult to employ in urban settings, but are also quite expensive. in addition, models appropriate for urban settings are difficult to apply in rural settings with few resources, and vice versa. finally, modern technologies for communication are used far too rarely in health education, in the improvement of self care, and to assist in the delivery of care. the role of the private sector in the provision of health care has grown rapidly, and in many countries, the private sectors are responsible for most of the care available or provided. most of the national and regional (and mental) health policies, however, rarely mention the role of the private health care sector and even less frequently encourage specific patterns of collaboration between the private and public health sectors. the undergraduate education of students of health professions, in most parts of the world, still places major emphasis on the description of a few of the most serious forms of mental illness, while failing to equip the graduates with skills that would allow them to competently deal with common mental disorders found in a community practice setting. postgraduate education in psychiatry is not standardized and varies dramatically in length and in content, often failing to focus on areas of knowledge that will be particularly important in the work of psychiatrists working outside academic centers. because the expanding knowledge base is difficult to integrate adequately, training programs struggle to keep up, and there are increasing disparities in the knowledge and skills base in clinicians trained in various institutions around the world. teaching the knowledge and skills necessary to provide care within a system that is generally fragmented and underfunded, and which often exists separated from the rest of the general health care system, is generally lacking, even in training programs in the most developed nations. the effect of all the forces described above has been that the number of mental health professionals, already inadequate in most parts of the world, grows slower than the population and the need for care for mental health problems. this and other discrepancies in mental health resources are apparent in the pacific rim region. countries on the rim of the pacific ocean differ from one another in many ways. some are rich, others are among the poorest in the world. they have different traditions, cultures, religions, climates, geographical characteristics and population sizes. for the purposes of the present article we define the pacific rim region as including the world health organization (who) regions of south-east asia, western pacific, and the americas. as is readily apparent, (table 1) the pacific rim region is one of contrast. only 23% of the population of south-east asia lives where national mental health policies exist to provide a template to develop services. in the western pacific, 93.8% of the population is covered, while in the americas, it is only 64%. when one examines how these policies are translated into activity, we see that in the americas, 75% of the population has the availability of community-based care for mental health, but only 50% in south-east asia, and 67% in the western pacific (table 2). thus, it is clear that just having a mental health policy does not ensure that the population is covered. further, the nature and extent of community services varies widely within countries due to a wide range of factors, including socioeconomic status, age, gender, ethnic or racial background, and geographic location in urban, suburban, or rural settings. the difficulty in obtaining services also is illustrated in table 2. as can be seen, the national drug policies, which include definition of essential lists of psychotropic drugs, cover 91% of the countries in the americas, 100% of the countries in south-east asia and 85% in the western pacific (table 2). however, further analysis reveals that the availability of these medications at the primary care level is much lower. in the americas, it is 63%, essentially the same as south-east asia, whereas in the western pacific, it is 81.5%. thus, the fact that there are national policies does not mean that there are resources available to provide services to the population (table 2). this is true even though 90% of countries in south-east asia have a national budget for mental health care, 78% in the americas, and 59% in the western pacific. in addition, lists of essential medications do not usually include all of the most recent generations of medications for common mood or psychotic illnesses due to the cost of these newer drugs. another measure of availability of services relates the availability of mental health care facilities and treatment facilities (table 3). when one reviews the availability of mental health care in the various regions, the numbers do not appear to indicate a problem: 94% in the americas, 80% in south-east asia, and 78% in the western pacific. however, further review of the national presence of treatment facilities for severe mental disorders reveals that the numbers are much lower: only 62% in the americas versus 44% in south-east asia and 52% in the western pacific (table 3). another illustration of the availability of services is availability of psychiatric beds (table 4). in the americas there are 2.6 beds per 10,000, while in the western pacific, there is one bed per 10,000, and in south-east asia, only 0.33 per 10,000, slightly lower than in africa. further, due to tremendous local variability in personnel, facilities, medications, supplies, and coordination with general health care for those needing mental health treatments, these figures clearly overestimate the availability of first-rate care. regional disparities are also apparent when considering the availability of workforce (table 4). when examining the number of psychiatrists per 100,000 people, we find that in the americas there are two. in the usa, however, the figure is 14 16 per 100,000, which substantially biases that overall average. in south-east asia, there are 0.2 psychiatrists per 100,000; less than anywhere in the world, except for africa. in the western pacific there are almost no psychiatrists on average, at 0.3 per 100,000, and this number is also biased by very high numbers in countries such as japan and australia. we must also consider the distribution of psychiatric nurses per 100,000 people. as shown in table 4, south-east asia has fewer psychiatric nurses than africa; the western pacific overall is only slightly better at 0.5, while the americas have 2.6. similar problems exist when we examine the number of psychologists or social workers (table 4). thus, reviewing who data shows that there are substantial economic barriers, systems deficits, and workforce barriers to individuals receiving appropriate psychiatric treatment in pacific rim countries. this is a critical problem that overwhelms many countries, even a country as wealthy as the usa, where many segments of the population have inadequate access to any treatment. for example, only 50% of individuals with a depressive episode in any one year receive treatment from any source in the usa and only 20% of children or adolescents needing a psychiatric evaluation actually receive one. we know that the percentages are much lower in countries with significantly greater deficiencies in resources for providing treatment. we alluded above to the key issue which relates to the important role that ethnicity and culture play in the presentation of psychiatric illness, stigmatization, willingness to seek treatment, and the relationship with clinicians as treatment is initiated and continues. ethnicity refers to a common heritage shared by a particular group, including history, language, rituals, preferences for music and food. historical experiences are pivotal to understanding ethnic identity and current health status. culture is also defined as a common heritage, but the emphasis is on a set of beliefs, norms, and values. it refers, as well, to the shared and largely learned attributes of a group of people. a key aspect of any culture is that it is dynamic. it continually changes and is influenced both by people's beliefs and the demands of the environment. in today's global environment, immigrants from different parts of the world arrive in other countries daily with their own culture and ethnic background, but they begin to adapt through the process of acculturation, that is, the socialization process by which minority members gradually learn and adopt selective elements of the dominant culture. the dominant culture is itself also transformed by its interaction with minority groups. due to these well described societal phenomena, it is abundantly clear that systems of care and methods of treatment that are developed must not only utilize information from the most recent advances, but must also adapt treatment systems and methods to meet the needs flowing from the local cultural and ethnic milieu. for example, while mental disorders are found worldwide and while we know that schizophrenia and bipolar disorder may have similar symptom profiles and rates across continents, diagnosis can be extremely challenging, even for the most gifted clinician, because the manifestations of many mental disorders vary with age, gender, ethnicity and culture. we are faced each day with the challenge of communication and interpretation within a culture; when patients and clinician come from different cultures the situation is even more complex. the solution to this challenge rests both with the patient and the clinician, and in their dynamic interactions, but the clinician must take the lead in considering this matter. patients from one culture may manifest and communicate symptoms in a way that is poorly understood in the culture of the clinician. in some cultures, words for states such as depression or anxiety are absent, but this does not mean that those individuals do not experience depression or anxiety. it is clear, therefore, that culture and social context, while not the only determinants, shape the mental health of populations and alter the types of mental health services they use, even within a single country or local region. cultural misunderstandings between patient and clinician, clinician bias, in addition to the fragmentation and insufficiency of mental health services deter many people from minority ethnic or cultural backgrounds from accessing and utilizing care. in addition, cultural and social factors may contribute to the causation of mental illness. they are not the same, however, for all disorders. the prevalence of schizophrenia, for example, is similar throughout the world, at approximately 1% of the population. in contrast, cultural and social context weigh much more heavily in the causation and presentation of depression. prevalence rates for major depression vary from 2% to 19% across countries. given the wide diversity of ethnicity and culture across the pacific rim region, it is clear that this is another major issue that must be taken into account when developing service systems and providing treatment. the role of family factors, coping styles, treatment seeking, trust in clinicians, stigma, immigration, overall health status, culture of the clinician, communication, clinician bias, and stereotyping, all must be taken into account. improving services in the pacific rim also relies on excellence in training the next generation of psychiatric clinicians. while who has found that psychiatric training programs exist in nearly every country in the pacific rim, there is little information available regarding the quality of such training or the resources available to those in training. further, the structure and content of training is highly variable across the world, and is influenced not only by resource availability, but also substantially by culture. as noted above, historically there has been little, if any, attention devoted during training to learning the knowledge and skills required, not only to diagnose and treat psychiatric disorders, but also to the cultural aspects of psychiatric practice. there is a growing body of work regarding cultural and transcultural aspects of psychiatry, but in an educational system that is incredibly variable in length, educators have regularly decided that training resources are too few to devote much attention to this component. this is a problem of the greatest magnitude, not only in areas of the world with few training resources, but also in developed countries with more time and resources available for training. given the scope of this problem, it is not surprising that education for young psychiatrists and other mental health professionals is commonly devoid of content regarding the application of the cultural and transcultural psychiatric knowledge base in the design of new models for care delivery. it is then clear that there are major systems challenges that must be addressed as we seek to improve the access to high quality care for all of our citizens and improve our training programs. and the ability to expand our knowledge base and appropriately transmit this to the next generation of psychiatrists is, as discussed, only part of the array of problems that must be overcome. the elements of new strategies for the development of mental health care systems are becoming apparent, but it is difficult to anticipate easy agreement across nationalities, even regarding the basic principals. such principals, however, might include integrated care for individuals with mental and physical illness, appropriate changes in the relationships between family and social service supports, provision for humane care of the severely impaired, and the appropriate development of resources and definition of which entities will provide those resources. implementation of a new model would require a variety of changes, not only in the treatment system, but also in our training programs; not only for all mental health clinicians, but also for other health care clinicians. any new system of care must take into account the high prevalence of comorbidity of physical and psychiatric illnesses to develop a truly integrated system of care. in addition, by utilizing the growth of patient and family advocacy groups, any new system must appropriately foster the development of more resources, not only regarding clinical care, but also for political advocacy. it goes without saying that without appropriate government, health care industry, and employer involvement in the development of a care system as primary stake holders, whatever model is developed will prove to be less effective than desired. it is, of course, essential to develop a system of care appropriate to the changing global environment for a variety of obvious reasons. such a system would allow for more appropriate planning and utilization of resources. in addition, using a "best practice" or an "evidence-based" approach, designed, tested, and modified locally with the appropriate attention to local traditions, culture, and ethnicity to determining care protocols, the field would more readily take advantage of optimal approaches based on present and evolving knowledge. further, knowledge gained from treatment effectiveness research in such new systems would clearly advance the field and lead to even better use of resources into the future. it goes without saying that knowledge gained from these endeavors must become integrated into psychiatric training curricula, with an increased emphasis on gaining skills in designing locally rooted new systems of care. a variety of initiatives title: practicing what we preach: teaching psychiatric mental health student nurses to care for themselves
display_name: Practicing What We Preach: Teaching Psychiatric–Mental Health Student Nurses to Care For Themselves
abstract: it is well known that stress has a profoundly negative impact on the physical, mental, and spiritual health of nurses. in addition, undergraduate nursing students experience a tremendous amount of stress as a result of their academic and clinical requirements. in the current study, new self-care activities were introduced in an undergraduate psychiatric mental health nursing course at a midsize, teaching-intensive university over the course of four academic semesters. thematic analysis was conducted using qualitative feedback from 79 students who completed standard university course evaluations, and four major themes emerged: stress levels , use of self-care strategies and coping skills , self-reflection , and perception of instructor . overall, students found value in self-care activities that have potential to reduce burnout, increase retention, and improve student and patient outcomes. therefore, a proactive approach should be taken early in undergraduate programs to provide education to nursing students about strategies to combat the deleterious effects of stress and promote self-care. [ journal of psychosocial nursing and mental health services, 58 (6), 40 45.]

title: managing the violent patient: a guide for psychologists and other mental health professionals.
display_name: Managing the violent patient: A guide for psychologists and other mental health professionals.
abstract: being threatened, harassed, attacked, or confronted by a patient with a weapon is becoming more common and is likely to occur at some point in a mental health professional's career.effective violence management programs can reduce the incidence of violence.yet, few resources have been provided to assist psychologists and other mental health professionals to deal with aggressive patients.the authors offer strategies for the management of aggressive behavior that can be implemented to empower practitioners to take precautions when necessary in a quick and efficient manner when dealing with violent and potentially violent patients.what would you do if your next patient were violent?are you prepared to handle a violent patient?assume your next patient arrives for a scheduled session and you notice a gun in the patient's briefcase.what would you do?or what if your next patient discloses a plan to injure a coworker and threatens harm to you and your loved ones if the plan is disclosed to anyone, including authorities?how would you handle these situations on a short-or long-term basis?rapid and efficient management of violent and potentially violent patients is a critical skill.violence management is needed by inpatient and outpatient mental health professionals in this era of managed care (i.e., minimal inpatient stays, limited and inexperienced staffing).the pervasiveness of aggression in acute psychiatric and other mental health settings has been documented.employees staffing one urban psychiatric emergency service identified 99 of 1,806 consecutive patients as violent or potentially violent (beck, white, & gage, 1991).a survey of 300 independent practitioners revealed that 81% experienced at least one incident of patient physical attack, verbal abuse, or other harassment (tryron, 1986).armed police in acute psychiatric facilities and pharmacies, panic buttons, and metal detector searches of patients have become the norm (mcculloch, mcniel, binder, & hatcher, 1986).psychologists and other staff often have little or no training regarding the management of potentially violent patients.we

abstract: in may 1987 the veterans administration established the homeless chronically mentally ill veterans program at 43 sites to provide outreach, health care, and residential rehabilitation services. intake assessment data on 10,529 homeless veterans screened as potential candidates for clinical services during the program's first 11 months are presented. with a median age of 40, the homeless veterans were considerably younger than veterans in the general u.s. population. more had served in the vietnam era than in other military eras. almost three-fifths were white, and a third were black; more than 40 percent were receiving some form of public support. almost half manifested one or more severe psychiatric symptoms at screening, and almost two-thirds had previously been hospitalized for either a psychiatric or a substance abuse problem.
